analogy.p: Imagine the history of life as a huge book where most of the pages were written in soft pencil. Over time many pages have been rubbed out (geological activity), many were never written at all (soft-bodied organisms leave no trace), and a few were pressed in stone so that they survive (fossils). Readers can work out the story from the pages that remain, but must accept gaps. The analogy breaks down because a book has an author and a fixed order of pages, whereas the fossil record is found in scattered pieces whose order scientists have to work out from rock layers and other evidence.
analogy.t: The torn-out pages of a library book

bullets: Fossils are found in **rocks** (sedimentary rocks especially), not just on the surface; they can be dug out of cliffs, quarries and mines.
A fossil is not always the original bone or shell: it may be a **mineral copy** of it, or just a **trace** such as a footprint.
**Evidence for evolution:** fossils of older organisms are often simpler or different from living ones, and sequences of fossils show gradual change over time.
Fossils also show **extinct species** that no longer exist, proving that species can disappear.
Scientists use the **depth of the rock layer** to compare ages: in undisturbed rock the deeper layers are older.
Link to other topics: fossils support Darwin's theory (Theories of evolution), and extinction links to environmental change and biodiversity.
core.h: What fossils are and why they matter
core.p: **Fossils** are the **remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks**. They are the most important direct evidence we have for how life on Earth has changed, because they show what ancient organisms looked like and when they lived. By comparing fossils from different ages we can learn **how much or how little organisms have changed as life developed on Earth**. The fossil record supports Darwin's theory of evolution but is incomplete, which is why this topic is also about why gaps exist.

bullets: **Ice (glaciers):** too cold for decay microorganisms to work, so whole animals, such as mammoths, have been preserved.
**Peat bogs:** waterlogged, acidic and short of **oxygen**, so decay microbes cannot function and bodies are preserved.
**Amber (fossilised tree resin):** insects trapped in sticky resin are sealed from air and microbes and so do not decay.
**Tar pits:** thick tar prevents microbes and oxygen reaching bones.
Hard parts such as **teeth, bones and shells** decay far more slowly than soft tissue, so they are the parts most often found.
Rapid burial in sediment can cut off oxygen supply and slow decay as well.
Exam link: the conditions needed for **decay** are the same ones used in the decomposition required practical (temperature, moisture, oxygen).
core.h: Fossil formation 1: parts that have not decayed
core.p: One way fossils form is from **parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent**. Decay is carried out by microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) that need **warmth, moisture and oxygen** to be active. If one of these is missing, the microbes cannot break the body down, so tissue survives for a very long time. The question often asks you to name the condition that is missing for a given example, so learn the pairing.

bullets: Step 1: The organism dies and is **buried quickly** in sediment (often at the bottom of a lake or sea).
Step 2: Soft tissues rot away, leaving hard parts (bone, teeth, shell).
Step 3: As the hard parts decay, **minerals replace** them particle by particle, keeping the shape and often fine detail.
Step 4: The layers of sediment above build up, press down and harden into **rock**.
Step 5: Millions of years later, erosion or digging **exposes the fossil**.
The fossil is therefore made of rock minerals, not of the original material: that is why it is described as being replaced by minerals.
Quick burial is important: it protects the remains from scavengers and from the oxygen that supports decay.
core.p: Most fossils of hard parts form when **parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay**. After an organism dies it is covered by sediment such as mud or sand. As the original material (bone or shell) slowly breaks down, **dissolved minerals from the water in the sediment** seep in and take its place, so a hard rock copy of the original structure is made. The sediment around it gradually turns into rock under pressure over millions of years.

bullets: **Footprints:** made in soft mud or sand which later hardens and is covered by new sediment, preserving the print.
**Burrows:** tunnels made by animals that are filled with sediment that hardens, leaving a cast of the burrow.
**Rootlet traces:** the pattern left by plant roots growing in soil, showing there was land vegetation.
Trace fossils show **behaviour** (walking, running, digging), which body fossils cannot.
They can be used to estimate **size, speed and group behaviour** (for example, parallel tracks suggest herds).
Be ready to name all three formation routes in order in a 3 mark question.
core.p: The third route in the specification is **preserved traces of organisms**. These are fossils which show the activity of an organism rather than its body. Examples given are **footprints, burrows and rootlet traces**. Soft mud or sand records the shape of the trace, which is then covered and hardened into rock. Trace fossils can tell scientists about how an animal moved, how big it was and how it lived, even when no bones survive.

bullets: **Soft-bodied organisms** (jellyfish-like creatures, worms, bacteria) decay quickly and have no bones or shells to leave fossils.
**Geological activity**, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, folding and heating and crushing of rock, destroys fossils that were already formed.
Most organisms die and are **scavenged or decay completely** and never become fossils.
Fossils are only found if rocks of the right age are **exposed** and someone **discovers** them.
Therefore we cannot be certain how life began; there is no conclusive fossil evidence of the very first life.
Therefore **gaps** exist in evolutionary sequences, though new discoveries keep filling them.
Higher tier thinking: absence of a fossil is not evidence that an organism did not exist.
core.h: Why the fossil record is incomplete
core.p: The fossil record has **gaps**, so it cannot give us a complete picture of life's history. The specification states that **many early forms of life were soft-bodied organisms, so have left few traces behind**, and **what traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity**. This is why scientists **cannot be certain about how life began on Earth**. An exam answer should always include both reasons: soft bodies and geological destruction.

bullets: Fossils of the **same type of organism from different layers** show the gradual change of features over time (e.g. gradual change in limb structure).
They show the **timing** of when groups first appeared and when they became extinct.
They give clues about **past environments** (marine fossils in a desert show the area was once under water).
Fossils show that many species that lived in the past **no longer exist**.
Scientists estimate age from the **rock layer** and (in later study) from radioactive dating, but at GCSE you mainly use position in the strata.
Interpret evidence: always say what the evidence **supports** rather than 'proves'.
Link to classification: fossils help scientists decide how organisms are related.
core.p: Fossils tell us **how much or how little organisms have changed** over time. By lining up fossils from different rock layers, scientists can build a sequence showing gradual change in features such as limb length or skull shape. Some species appear to have changed very little over huge periods of time, while others changed a lot, or disappeared. This evidence, together with DNA comparison, is used to construct evolutionary trees.

bullets: **Deeper = older** (assuming the rocks have not been folded or flipped by geological activity).
Species found only in lower layers have become extinct; species in only upper layers appeared later.
Age (years) = depth ÷ rate of deposition, if the rate is constant. Example: 15 m at 2 mm per 100 years: 15 000 mm ÷ 2 mm = 7 500 sets of 100 years = 750 000 years.
Convert units first (1 m = 1000 mm) before dividing.
The rate may have varied, so the answer is only an **estimate**.
Fossils found in several places in the same layer can be used to match the age of rocks in different locations.
core.h: Reading rock layers (strata) and dating by depth
core.p: In undisturbed sedimentary rock, **new layers are laid down on top of older ones**, so deeper fossils are older. Comparing the fossils found at different depths shows the order in which species appeared and disappeared. If a species is found in lower layers but not in higher layers, it has probably become **extinct** before the upper layers formed. Exam questions can give a deposition rate so you can estimate the age of a layer by calculation.

bullets: A species is extinct only when **all individuals have died** with none able to reproduce.
Extinction can be **gradual** (over many generations) or sudden after a major event.
Species most at risk are those with small populations, narrow habitat or limited variation.
Extinction is linked with natural selection: if no individuals have alleles suited to a changing environment, the species cannot survive.
Fossils of extinct species show which organisms disappeared and when.
A species is **endangered** when it is at risk of becoming extinct, which is why conservation is needed.
Link to ecology: loss of one species can affect others in the food web.
core.p: **Extinction** occurs when **there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive**. Many species of organisms that have lived on Earth have become extinct; scientists believe most species that ever existed no longer exist. Extinction is a natural process but it can also be accelerated by human activity. Fossils are the main evidence that extinction has happened in the past.

bullets: **Catastrophic events:** a huge volcanic eruption or an asteroid collision can change the climate quickly (dust blocking sunlight, cooling, loss of plants), so many species cannot adapt in time and die out. A large asteroid impact about 66 million years ago is widely linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs.
**Changes to the environment over geological time:** climate, sea level and land masses change slowly; species that cannot adapt through natural selection become extinct.
**New predators:** prey that have no defences against a new predator may be eaten faster than they can reproduce.
**New diseases:** a new pathogen may kill most of a population, especially if there is little genetic variation and so no resistance.
**New, more successful competitors:** a better-adapted species takes food and space, so the less well adapted species cannot get enough resources to survive and breed.
Often several causes act at once.
Humans cause extinctions today by hunting, habitat destruction, pollution and introducing alien species (see biodiversity).
core.p: The specification lists several causes of extinction, which you should be able to recall and apply to unfamiliar examples. They are: **catastrophic events** (for example volcanic eruptions or collisions with asteroids), **changes to the environment over geological time**, **new predators**, **new diseases**, and **new, more successful competitors**. A good answer links the cause to the effect on survival and reproduction, not just a list.

bullets: Mass extinction layers show a sudden loss of many types of fossils in the rock record.
Survivors often had features (small size, burrowing, flexible diet) that helped them endure.
After mass extinctions, surviving groups can evolve into new species through natural selection, because there is less competition (new niches become available).
Rapid change gives **less time** for natural selection to produce adaptation, so extinction is more likely.
Slow environmental change allows populations to evolve gradually.
Compare: the rate of extinction today is thought to be higher than normal due to human activity.
Evidence is always based on **fossil record**, which is incomplete, so dates and causes may be revised.
core.h: Mass extinctions and the pace of change
core.p: Some catastrophic events cause **mass extinctions**, where a large proportion of species die in a relatively short time. The fossil record shows that there have been several such events, followed by periods when surviving groups diversified (evolved into many new species) to fill the empty habitats. For GCSE you should link events such as asteroid collisions or major volcanic activity to rapid environmental change.

bullets: Sequences of fossils show **gradual change** in a feature over many millions of years.
Extinct species show that life has **not remained the same**.
Because the record is incomplete, the lack of a fossil for a link does not disprove the theory.
The discovery of more fossils since Darwin's time has strengthened the evidence base.
Scientists check conclusions by **peer review** and by comparing different types of evidence.
Fossils are a type of evidence that can be **checked** by other scientists examining the same specimens.
Link: antibiotic resistance gives evidence of evolution happening now; fossils give evidence of the past.
core.h: Fossils and the evidence for evolution
core.p: Taken together, fossils provide strong support for evolution. Older rock layers contain simpler or different organisms and newer layers contain organisms more like those living today, which is what we would predict if species have changed through natural selection. Where fossils of intermediate forms exist, they link older and newer groups. Fossils alone are not enough, so scientists combine them with DNA evidence, anatomy and observations of living species.

bullets: On a graph of species number against time, a sharp fall suggests a mass extinction; give start and end values to describe it.
On a diagram of strata, work out relative age from depth: deeper means older.
When asked to suggest a reason, choose from the five listed causes of extinction and use the information given in the question.
When asked 'why can't scientists be certain', mention soft bodies, destruction by geological activity and incomplete record.
When asked to **evaluate** evidence, mention strengths (physical evidence, can be examined) and limits (gaps, uncertain dating, interpretations).
For calculations on depth and time, convert units first and show the working.
core.h: Applying the ideas: interpreting data and graphs about fossils and extinction
core.p: Exam questions may give a table of fossil finds at different depths, a graph of the number of species over time, or a diagram of rock layers. The method is to read the data carefully, describe what it shows with numbers, and then use the ideas from this topic to explain it. Remember to include units, and make careful comments about what the evidence can and cannot show.

exam: **Know the three routes** to fossils: parts not decayed (a decay condition absent), replacement by minerals, preserved traces (footprints, burrows, rootlet traces).
**Decay conditions:** warmth, moisture and oxygen. Name the missing condition for ice (cold), peat bog (oxygen), amber (sealed from air).
**'Why can scientists not be certain how life began?'** (2 marks): early life was soft-bodied so left few traces; traces were mainly destroyed by geological activity.
**Extinction causes list:** catastrophic event (volcano/asteroid), environmental change over time, new predator, new disease, new competitor. Give one fact for each in a 5 mark answer.
**Define extinction** as no remaining individuals of a species alive.
**4 mark 'describe how a fossil forms':** quick burial → soft parts decay → minerals replace hard parts → rock forms/exposed. One mark per stage in order.
**Depth calculations:** convert metres to millimetres, divide by rate, state it is an estimate; show working for method marks.
**Graph questions:** quote values with units, give the overall trend and say what it suggests (e.g. mass extinction).
**Use 'supports' not 'proves'** when linking fossils to evolution; mention the record is incomplete.
**6 mark question:** combine natural selection (environment changes, no suitable alleles) with causes of extinction and evidence from fossils. Write in logical order.
**Link to other topics** such as decomposition and antibiotic resistance to show wide understanding.

mistakes.r: Fossils are remains, often replaced by minerals, or traces such as footprints; some are parts that did not decay because decay conditions were absent.
mistakes.w: Fossils are the bodies of dead animals turned to stone.

mistakes.r: Decay was prevented because a condition for decay (warmth, moisture or oxygen) was missing.
mistakes.w: The fossil didn't decay because it was old.

mistakes.r: Early life was soft-bodied, leaving few traces, and what traces there were were mainly destroyed by geological activity.
mistakes.w: There are few early fossils because they were small.

mistakes.r: Extinction means there are no remaining individuals of the species still alive.
Give a specific cause such as a catastrophic event (e.g. asteroid collision) changing the environment faster than they could adapt.
mistakes.w: Dinosaurs went extinct because they were not strong enough.

mistakes.r: Fossils provide evidence that supports evolution; say supports, and note the record is incomplete.
In undisturbed rock, deeper layers are older because newer layers are laid down on top.
It has gaps because few organisms become fossils and many fossils are destroyed or undiscovered.

summary: You must know how fossils form (parts that have not decayed because decay conditions are absent, replacement of parts by minerals, and preserved traces such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces), why the fossil record is incomplete, and what fossils tell us about how organisms have changed. You must also know what extinction is and its causes: catastrophic events, environmental change, new predators, diseases and competitors.

terms.d: The remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks.
When there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.
The breakdown of dead organisms by microorganisms, needing warmth, moisture and oxygen.
Particles of mud, sand or silt deposited in layers by water, which can bury organisms and later form rock.
The process in which parts of an organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, forming a rock copy.
A preserved sign of an organism's activity, such as a footprint, burrow or rootlet trace.
Layers of sedimentary rock; in undisturbed rock the deeper layers are older.
An organism without hard parts such as bones or shells, which leaves few fossil traces.
Processes such as earthquakes, volcanic activity and folding of rock that can destroy fossils.
A sudden major event, such as a volcanic eruption or asteroid collision, that can cause extinctions.
A time when a large proportion of species die out in a relatively short period.
Hardened tree resin that can preserve trapped organisms by sealing them from air and microbes.
Waterlogged, acidic ground with little oxygen where decay is very slow.
An organism that uses the same limited resources as another; a new, more successful one can cause extinction.
A diagram showing how organisms are related, based on evidence such as fossils and DNA.

worked.ans: Model answer: The animal dies and is quickly covered with sediment such as mud. The soft parts decay but the hard shell remains. As the shell decays, minerals dissolved in water replace it, particle by particle, keeping its shape. The sediment is compressed into rock, and millions of years later erosion exposes the fossil.
worked.q: [4 marks] Describe how a fossil of an animal's shell can form.
steps: Animal dies and is buried by sediment.
Soft parts decay leaving the shell.
Minerals replace the shell as it decays.
Sediment hardens into rock and fossil is exposed later.

worked.ans: Early life forms were soft-bodied so left few fossil traces, and the traces that did form were mainly destroyed by geological activity such as movement of rocks.
worked.q: [2 marks] Scientists cannot be certain how life on Earth began. Explain why.
steps: Early organisms were soft-bodied so left few traces.
Traces that formed were mainly destroyed by geological activity.

worked.ans: 750 000 years (an estimate, assuming a constant rate of deposition).
worked.q: [3 marks] A fossil is found 15 m below the surface. Rock forms at 2 mm every 100 years. Estimate the age of the fossil.
